clinicalPearls: The most common human enzyme defect, inherited in an X-linked pattern so that males are predominantly affected while heterozygous females show variable expression.
Most individuals are asymptomatic between episodes and present only with acute haemolysis triggered by oxidative stress.
Common triggers include certain infections, fava (broad) beans, and oxidant drugs such as some antimalarials, sulphonamides, and nitrofurantoin.
Acute haemolysis produces sudden pallor, jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue, typically 1-3 days after exposure to a trigger.
It is an important cause of neonatal jaundice, which can be severe and lead to kernicterus if unrecognised.
The blood film during a crisis may show bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies, with a rise in reticulocytes.
Enzyme activity assay is diagnostic but can be falsely normal during an acute crisis because young reticulocytes have higher enzyme levels, so retesting after recovery is advised.
Management centres on avoiding known triggers; acute severe haemolysis may require transfusion, and neonatal jaundice is managed with phototherapy or exchange transfusion as needed.
reference.pathophysiology: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway and generates NADPH, which maintains reduced glutathione in red cells. Deficiency impairs this antioxidant defence, so under oxidative stress haemoglobin is oxidised and denatured, precipitating as Heinz bodies within red cells. These damaged cells are removed by splenic macrophages (producing bite cells) and undergo intravascular haemolysis, resulting in episodic anaemia, jaundice, and haemoglobinuria.
additionalDifferentials: Other red cell enzyme defects (e.g. pyruvate kinase deficiency)
Drug- or toxin-induced haemolysis from other causes
Neonatal jaundice of other aetiology (ABO/Rh incompatibility, sepsis)
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative G6PD enzyme activity assay (repeat after recovery if measured during crisis)
Full blood count and reticulocyte count
Peripheral blood film for bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz body preparation
Markers of haemolysis: bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test to help exclude immune haemolysis
redFlags: Rapidly falling haemoglobin with haemodynamic compromise
Massive haemolysis with haemoglobinuria and acute kidney injury
Marked jaundice with lethargy or poor feeding in a neonate
Ongoing exposure to an unrecognised oxidative trigger
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals lead normal lives with trigger avoidance; haemolytic episodes are usually self-limiting once the trigger is removed, though neonatal jaundice and rare severe crises can cause serious harm if not promptly managed.
pitfalls: Interpreting a normal enzyme level during acute haemolysis as excluding the diagnosis
Failing to counsel families about drug, food, and infection triggers
Underestimating the risk of severe neonatal jaundice and kernicterus
Prescribing oxidant medications without checking G6PD status in at-risk populations
